name: COURT STAFF, COURT RECORDS, COURT DATES
safetyNote: Nothing here is legal advice. It tells you who does what in a courthouse and what you can do there. Nine of these questions say "in Michigan" because those rules are Michigan's own and other states do it differently. That difference is worth noticing: how a courtroom is run varies far more between states than who the people in it are.

questions.q: You need to file something or get a copy of your case file. Who handles that?

options.explanation: A judge decides cases. The paperwork lives with the clerk.
Your lawyer keeps a copy. The court's own file is at the clerk's office.
The prosecutor filed it and does not keep the court's copy of it.

questions.hint: Somebody in that building does nothing but paperwork.
questions.principle: The clerk's office keeps every court file, takes every filing, and collects fees. It is the front door of a courthouse. A clerk will tell you where a form goes and what a deadline is, and is not allowed to tell you what to write on it, which is a rule they work under rather than unhelpfulness.

keyPhrase.quote: The clerk's office holds the paperwork.
keyPhrase.gloss: Every filing goes through there.

scenario.setup: School trip. The class stops at a counter on the first floor.

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: What happens here?

lines.label: CLERK
lines.text: Everything filed in this building comes through us. Every file, every deadline.

scenario.note: Every filing, file and deadline in that building runs through the clerk's office.

questions.q: A bailiff tells everybody to stand when the judge walks in. What is a bailiff's job?

options.explanation: A bailiff is not assigned to one person. The job is the whole room.
A bailiff does not advise anybody about the case, including the judge.
The record is kept by the court reporter, not the bailiff.

questions.hint: Watch what a bailiff actually does all day.
questions.principle: A bailiff keeps order, calls cases, handles anybody in custody, and manages the room. Not on either side and not advising anybody. Titles differ by court, and in some Michigan courtrooms a court officer does the same work under a different name.

keyPhrase.quote: A bailiff runs the room, not the case.
keyPhrase.gloss: Order, not sides.

scenario.setup: Your family is in court for a relative's hearing. Everybody stands.

lines.label: BAILIFF
lines.text: All rise.

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: Is that a police officer?

scenario.note: A bailiff keeps order for the whole room, not safety for one person in it.

questions.q: Somebody sitting near the front of the courtroom types everything that gets said. Why is that person there?

options.text: To make a record of what happened.
To take notes for the judge.
options.explanation: A court reporter does not work for either side, including the bench.
The record is a written account of what was said. It does not judge anything.

options.text: To send updates to the lawyers.
options.explanation: Nothing gets sent out during a hearing. The record is made for afterward.

questions.hint: Somebody might need to know exactly what was said, months from now.
questions.principle: A court reporter makes a word-for-word record of what gets said. That record is what an appeal is built on and what anybody arguing about what happened has to work from. It exists so a hearing does not come down to whose memory is better.

keyPhrase.quote: Everything said gets written down.
keyPhrase.gloss: The record outlives everybody's memory.

scenario.setup: Back row of a courtroom with your cousin, twenty minutes in.

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: Why is that person typing the whole time?

lines.label: COUSIN
lines.text: So there's a record. If anybody appeals, that's what they use.

scenario.note: Everything said gets written down, and that record is what an appeal is built from.

questions.q: You are the defendant in a criminal case. The clerk, the bailiff and the court reporter all work at that courthouse. Which one is on your side?

options.text: The clerk, since the clerk helps you file.
options.explanation: A clerk being helpful about a form is not the same as being on your side.

options.text: The bailiff, since the bailiff keeps you safe.
options.explanation: A bailiff keeps order for the whole room, not safety for one person in it.

options.text: All of them, since they work for the court, not the state.
options.explanation: Court staff work for the process, which means for neither side.

questions.hint: Two people in a courtroom have sides. Neither one is staff.
questions.principle: Court staff work for the court, which means they work for the process rather than for either side. They are usually helpful and being helpful is not the same as being yours. The only person in that room whose job is your side is your defence lawyer.

keyPhrase.quote: Helpful is not the same as yours.
keyPhrase.gloss: Court staff work for the process.

scenario.setup: At home afterwards, talking about who was in the room.

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: The clerk was really helpful. Is she on our side?

lines.label: MOM
lines.text: She works for the court. That means neither side.

scenario.note: Court staff work for the process, which means they work for neither side.

questions.q: You get put on probation. What is a probation officer's job?

options.text: Checking whether you follow the conditions.
Helping you find a job and stay on track.
options.explanation: A probation officer may genuinely want you to succeed. The job is still checking and reporting.

options.text: Deciding whether you go to jail.
options.explanation: A probation officer reports. A judge decides what happens next.
Your lawyer argues your side. A probation officer does not.

questions.hint: The word probation comes with a list attached.
questions.principle: Probation is a court order with conditions on it, and a probation officer's job is to check whether those conditions are being followed and to report to the court. Many are decent people who genuinely want somebody to succeed. That does not change who they report to.

keyPhrase.quote: A probation officer checks and reports.
keyPhrase.gloss: Kind is not the same as on your side.

scenario.setup: Your cousin finished probation last year and is explaining it.

lines.label: COUSIN
lines.text: She was decent to me. But her job was checking I did what the order said.

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: So not, like, a support worker.

scenario.note: A probation officer checks whether a court order is being followed, and reports.

questions.q: You tell your probation officer you missed a drug test. Who else finds out?

options.text: Nobody, if the officer decides to let it go.
options.explanation: A probation officer's job is to report to the court. Letting it go is not part of that job.
Your lawyer is not in that loop. Reports go to the court.
Notes made by a probation officer are made for the court and end up there.

questions.hint: Ask who the probation officer answers to.
questions.principle: A probation officer reports to the court. What you say gets written down and can end up in a report a judge reads. There is no confidentiality here, and that is the difference between a probation officer and a lawyer: one keeps what you say, one passes it on.

keyPhrase.quote: Nothing you tell a probation officer is private.
keyPhrase.gloss: It goes to the court.

scenario.setup: A youth worker at the community centre is answering questions.

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: If somebody tells their probation officer they slipped up, where does that go?

lines.label: STAFF
lines.text: Into a report the judge can read. That's what the job is.

scenario.note: Nothing said to a probation officer is private. Reporting is the job.

questions.q: Your probation officer says it is fine to skip next month's meeting. Who has to make that official?

options.text: Nobody. The officer saying it is enough.
options.explanation: A probation officer can decide day-to-day things and cannot rewrite a court order.
Your lawyer can ask the court to change something. Agreeing is not changing.
The office that supervises you follows the order. It does not write it.

questions.hint: Who wrote the conditions in the first place?
questions.principle: Probation conditions come from a court order, so only the court changes them. A probation officer can decide how to handle day-to-day things and cannot rewrite the order. If something needs to change for real, it goes back to the judge. Conditions do get changed, and probation does get ended early, through the court.

keyPhrase.quote: Only the court changes a court order.
keyPhrase.gloss: Everything else is somebody's say-so.

scenario.setup: Your uncle, about somebody at work who is on probation.

lines.label: UNCLE
lines.text: His officer told him to skip a month. He got it in writing anyway.

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: Why bother?

scenario.note: Only the court changes a court order. Everything else is somebody's say-so.

questions.q: Your probation officer is easy to talk to and you trust them. Is anything you say to a probation officer private?

options.text: Yes, the same as with a lawyer.
options.explanation: Your lawyer has a duty to keep what you say. A probation officer has a duty to report it.

options.text: Yes, if you ask them to keep it quiet.
options.explanation: Asking for something to stay quiet does not create confidentiality that was never there.

options.text: Only the parts not about your case.
options.explanation: Nothing is carved out. A probation officer's job is reporting, whatever the subject is.

questions.hint: One person in this system has a duty to keep your secrets, and it is not this one.
questions.principle: Nothing you say to a probation officer is confidential. That is not a trick or a failure on their part. Their job is to report to the court, and reporting is the opposite of keeping. Your lawyer is the only person in the process with a duty to keep what you say.

keyPhrase.quote: Only your lawyer keeps what you say.
keyPhrase.gloss: A probation officer's job is to pass it on.

scenario.setup: A friend is worried about somebody in her family.

lines.label: FRIEND
lines.text: Can you tell a probation officer something off the record?

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: No. That's what a lawyer's for.

scenario.note: Your own lawyer is the only person in the process who has to keep what you say.

questions.q: Your aunt has to testify, but she does not speak enough English to follow the hearing. What does the court provide?

options.explanation: Courts appoint interpreters. Nobody is expected to arrive with one.
A translation afterward does not help somebody follow a hearing as it happens.

options.text: A delay until she learns enough English.
options.explanation: Cases do not wait for somebody to learn English. An interpreter is how they take part now.

questions.hint: She has to be able to follow it to take part in it.
questions.principle: Courts appoint an interpreter when somebody asks for one or when the court decides one is needed for that person to take part meaningfully. It covers parties, witnesses, and other people with a real interest in the case. Sign language interpreting runs under separate rules.

keyPhrase.quote: The court provides an interpreter.
keyPhrase.gloss: Asking for one is normal.

scenario.setup: Your aunt has to give evidence. She does not follow much English.

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: She doesn't understand any of this.

lines.label: CLERK
lines.text: Tell the judge. We'll get an interpreter.

scenario.note: Courts appoint an interpreter when somebody cannot follow the hearing in English.

questions.q: In Michigan your grandmother has to testify and your cousin speaks both languages. Can your cousin be her interpreter?

options.text: Only if the court appoints your cousin.

options.explanation: Interpreting at a doctor's office and interpreting in court are different things with different rules.

options.text: Yes, if your grandmother asks for your cousin.
options.explanation: The person testifying does not choose the interpreter. The court does.

options.text: No. Family members are never allowed.
options.explanation: Family is not barred outright. In a rare language a court may appoint somebody it decides is capable.

questions.hint: Somebody has to decide, and it is not the family.
questions.principle: The court decides who interprets. Michigan courts appoint a certified interpreter whenever practicable, then a qualified one, and only if neither is available may the court appoint somebody it decides is capable. So a family member is not barred outright and is not the default either. The reason is that an interpreter has to be neutral, and family rarely is.

keyPhrase.quote: The court picks the interpreter.
keyPhrase.gloss: Neutral matters more than convenient.

scenario.setup: A neighbour is going to court as a witness and is worried about the language.

lines.label: NEIGHBOUR
lines.text: My daughter can come and translate for me.

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: I think the court picks who does that.

scenario.note: The court decides who interprets, because an interpreter has to be neutral.

questions.q: In a Michigan criminal case, who pays for a court interpreter?

options.text: Nobody. It is free to the person who needs it.

options.explanation: In a Michigan criminal case nobody is charged for an interpreter, including the person who needs one.
Neither side pays. In a criminal case the cost is not passed to anybody.

options.text: The family, if the court asks them to.
options.explanation: Since a court rule change in November 2025, a Michigan court cannot pass interpreter costs to a party in a criminal case.

questions.hint: Being able to follow your own case is not a thing you buy.
questions.principle: In a Michigan criminal case the court pays and cannot make a party pay it back. That has been true since a court rule change in November 2025. In civil cases a court can still order a party to cover some or all of an interpreter's cost, which is one more place where criminal and civil work differently.

keyPhrase.quote: In a criminal case it costs you nothing.
keyPhrase.gloss: Civil cases can work differently.

scenario.setup: A community meeting about going to court. Somebody puts a hand up.

lines.label: NEIGHBOUR
lines.text: What does an interpreter cost?

lines.label: STAFF
lines.text: In a criminal case, nothing. The court covers it.

lines.label: YES
lines.text: Nobody skips asking for an interpreter over money.

lines.label: NO
lines.text: Somebody goes without because the family was scared of a bill.

questions.q: An interpreter is working in a Michigan courtroom. What is that person's job?

options.text: Saying exactly what each person said.

options.explanation: An interpreter repeats what was said. Explaining would be adding something nobody said.
An interpreter is an impartial officer of the court and is not on either side.
Summarising means leaving things out, and an interpreter is not allowed to leave anything out.

questions.hint: Ask what would go wrong if an interpreter improved somebody's answer.
questions.principle: An interpreter has to render what was said completely and accurately, adding nothing and leaving nothing out, and is an impartial officer of the court. Not on either side, not explaining, not smoothing anything over. The point is to put somebody in the same position as an English speaker in the same seat, which means the same words and not better ones.

keyPhrase.quote: An interpreter says it, and does not improve it.
keyPhrase.gloss: Nothing added, nothing left out.

scenario.setup: Watching a hearing where a witness is speaking through an interpreter.

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: She said way more than that.

lines.label: COUSIN
lines.text: They have to say it exactly. Nothing added, nothing cut.

scenario.note: An interpreter says it exactly. Nothing added, nothing left out, nothing improved.

questions.q: What is a bail bondsman?

options.text: A business that posts bond for a fee.
A court official who handles bonds.
options.explanation: A bondsman is a private business. Nobody at the courthouse works for one.

options.text: A lender the court assigns you.
options.explanation: No court assigns you a bondsman. Whether to use one is a decision a family makes.

options.text: A lawyer who specialises in bond.
options.explanation: A bondsman is not a lawyer and cannot give legal advice.

questions.hint: Ask who makes money when somebody uses one.
questions.principle: A bail bondsman is a private business. It posts a bond so somebody can get out, and it charges a fee for doing that. Nobody in the courthouse works for a bondsman and no bondsman works for the courthouse. Whether to use one is a decision a family makes, the way any other money decision gets made.

keyPhrase.quote: A bondsman is a business.
keyPhrase.gloss: Not part of the court, not on anybody's side.

scenario.setup: An advert on a bus stop bench near the courthouse.

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: Is that a court thing?

lines.label: MOM
lines.text: No. That's a company. They charge to post it for you.

scenario.note: A bail bondsman is a private business, not part of the court.

questions.q: Your family pays a bondsman a fee to post a bond. Do you get that money back at the end?

options.text: Yes, if you go to every hearing.
options.explanation: Going to every hearing is what you agreed to do. It does not earn the fee back.

options.text: Yes, if the case gets dropped.
options.explanation: A dismissal ends the case. It does not refund a business its price for a service already provided.

options.text: Half of it, at the end of the case.
options.explanation: None of it comes back. A fee is a price, not a deposit.

questions.hint: A fee is a price for a service, not a deposit.
questions.principle: A bondsman's fee is what the business charges. It is not a deposit and it does not come back, even if the case is dropped and even if every hearing gets attended. That is different from bond money paid to the court directly, which can come back at the end after anything owed is taken out of it.

keyPhrase.quote: A fee is not a deposit.
keyPhrase.gloss: It does not come back.

scenario.setup: Kitchen table, months after a relative's case finished.

lines.label: MOM
lines.text: So when do we get the fee back?

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: We don't. That part was the price.

scenario.note: A bondsman's fee is a price for a service. It does not come back.

questions.q: Your family cannot reach the bondsman and your court date is tomorrow. Who is responsible for you showing up?

options.explanation: A bondsman has money riding on you appearing and may call. That is the business protecting itself, not a duty owed to you.
Your lawyer will remind you and is not the one ordered to appear.
Whoever posted the bond loses money if you miss. The order to appear is still on you.

questions.hint: Ask whose name is on the order to appear.
questions.principle: The order to appear is on you. A bondsman has a financial interest in you turning up and may call or come looking, and that is the business protecting its money rather than a duty owed to you. If nobody calls and nobody reminds you, the court date is still yours.

keyPhrase.quote: Showing up is yours.
keyPhrase.gloss: Nobody else is responsible for it.

scenario.setup: Your cousin has court in the morning and nobody can reach anyone.

lines.label: COUSIN
lines.text: Nobody's answering. Do I still go?

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: Yeah. It's your date either way.

lines.label: YES
lines.text: He is there in the morning.

lines.label: NO
lines.text: He waits for a phone call instead of turning up.

questions.q: In Michigan, who decides how much a bond is?

options.explanation: A bondsman charges a fee for posting whatever number the court already set.
The prosecutor can ask for an amount. Asking is not setting.
The jail holds people. It has no say in the amount.

questions.hint: Somebody with authority over the case sets it, not somebody selling a service.
questions.principle: A judge sets bond, and in Michigan a district court magistrate can set it too for certain offences when the chief judge has authorised it. A magistrate is not a judge and does a specific list of things a chief judge signs off on. A bondsman only decides what to charge for posting whatever number the court already set.

keyPhrase.quote: The court sets the amount. The bondsman sets the fee.
keyPhrase.gloss: Two different numbers from two different people.

scenario.setup: School trip. The class watches a first appearance.

lines.label: MAGISTRATE
lines.text: Bond is set at five thousand, ten percent.

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: Who is that? That's not the judge.

scenario.note: A judge sets bond, and in Michigan a magistrate can too for certain offences.

questions.q: Your cousin has a hearing next week and you want to sit in. What do you usually need to get in?

options.text: Nothing. Most hearings are open to anybody.

options.explanation: Court is held in public. Nobody has to let you in.
You do not have to be connected to a case to watch it.

options.text: Your cousin's lawyer to sign you in.
options.explanation: Access does not run through the lawyers. You walk in.

questions.hint: Ask who court is being held in front of.
questions.principle: Court is held in public. You can walk into a courthouse, go through security, and sit in on a hearing you have nothing to do with. Some things are closed, and they are exceptions rather than the rule. That openness is not a courtesy. It is how everybody gets to see whether the system does what it says.

keyPhrase.quote: Court happens in public.
keyPhrase.gloss: You can walk in and watch.

scenario.setup: Your cousin has a hearing next week.

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: Can I come watch, or do I need permission?

lines.label: COUSIN
lines.text: Just turn up. Court's open.

lines.label: YES
lines.text: You are in the room when it happens.

lines.label: NO
lines.text: Nobody goes, because everybody assumed they were not allowed.

questions.q: In Michigan, are juvenile court hearings open to the public?

options.text: No, juvenile hearings are always closed.
options.explanation: Michigan juvenile hearings on the formal calendar are open. It is the records that are closed here.
The family does not control who can attend a hearing.

options.text: Only the ones for older teenagers.
options.explanation: Age does not decide whether a hearing is open.

questions.hint: This surprises most people, including most adults.
questions.principle: Michigan juvenile proceedings on the formal calendar and preliminary hearings are open to the public. Anybody can sit in the gallery. Most people assume the opposite because juvenile **records** are closed here, and those are two different things. The hearing is open. The file is not.

keyPhrase.quote: The hearing is open. The file is not.
keyPhrase.gloss: Two different questions with two different answers.

scenario.setup: The family arguing about it in the car outside.

lines.label: MOM
lines.text: They won't let us in, it's a juvenile thing.

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: I think we can go in. It's the records that are private.

lines.label: YES
lines.text: The family is in the room for the hearing.

lines.label: NO
lines.text: Everybody waits in the car park for no reason.

questions.q: When can a Michigan judge close part of a juvenile hearing to the public?

options.text: While a child or a victim is testifying.

options.explanation: Closing a courtroom is narrow and has to be justified. It is not a matter of preference.
A parent can ask, and the court decides, and only for testimony.

options.text: For the whole hearing, if the case is serious.
options.explanation: How serious a case is does not close a courtroom. The exception is about protecting a witness while they speak.

questions.hint: The exception is about protecting one person while they speak.
questions.principle: A Michigan court can close part of a juvenile hearing while a child or a victim testifies, on a motion from a party or the victim, to protect that person. The judge weighs the nature of the proceeding and what that witness wants. It is a narrow exception for a stretch of testimony, not a way to close a whole hearing.

keyPhrase.quote: Closing is narrow and it is about testimony.
keyPhrase.gloss: The rest of the hearing stays open.

scenario.setup: Mid-hearing, the judge speaks to the gallery.

lines.label: JUDGE
lines.text: I'm clearing the room for this witness. We'll bring everybody back after.

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: Are we done?

scenario.note: A judge can close part of a juvenile hearing while a child or a victim testifies.

questions.q: You are sitting in the gallery watching a case. What are you allowed to do in there?

options.text: Speak up if something is wrong.
options.explanation: Speaking from the gallery can get you removed and can be treated as contempt.
Open to the public does not mean open to recording. Assume you cannot unless somebody says you can.

options.text: Ask the judge a question afterward.
options.explanation: A judge does not take questions from the gallery.

questions.hint: Open means you can be there. It does not mean you are taking part.
questions.principle: Watching is not taking part. From the gallery you sit, listen and leave. Speaking out can get you removed and can be treated as contempt. Rules about phones, recording and what you can bring in vary courthouse to courthouse, and the safe assumption is that recording is not allowed unless somebody says it is.

keyPhrase.quote: You can be there. You are not taking part.
keyPhrase.gloss: Watch, listen, stay quiet.

scenario.setup: Back row, and something just got said that was not right.

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: That's not what happened.

lines.label: BAILIFF
lines.text: Outside, please.

lines.label: YES
lines.text: You save it for the hallway afterward.

lines.label: NO
lines.text: You get removed and miss the rest of it.

questions.q: You want to look at the file on an adult criminal case. What do you have to show to see it?

options.text: Nothing. Most of it is public.
That you are related to somebody in it.
options.explanation: You do not have to be connected to a case to read the file.
No reason is required for an adult criminal file. Most of it is simply public.
You can ask at the counter yourself. No lawyer is involved.

questions.hint: Court is public, and so is most of the paperwork.
questions.principle: Adult criminal case files are mostly public. You can go to the clerk's office and ask to see one. Some things inside a file are sealed, and the file as a whole is open. This is the same principle as an open courtroom, applied to paper.

keyPhrase.quote: Adult case files are mostly public.
keyPhrase.gloss: You do not need a reason.

scenario.setup: The clerk's counter, with a case number on a scrap of paper.

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: Do I have to explain why I want it?

lines.label: CLERK
lines.text: No. Have a seat and I'll pull it.

scenario.note: Adult criminal files are mostly public, and you do not need a reason to read one.

questions.q: In Michigan, who can look at a juvenile's court record?

options.text: Only people with a real reason.
Anybody, the same as an adult case.
options.explanation: Adult files are mostly public. Michigan juvenile files are not, and have not been since 2021.

options.text: Only the kid and the parents.
options.explanation: The list is wider than the family. It includes lawyers, police, the court and others.
They are not sealed absolutely. People with a real reason can be allowed access.

questions.hint: It is narrower than adult files and wider than nobody.
questions.principle: Michigan juvenile case records are open only to people the court finds have a legitimate interest. That list includes the young person, a parent, a lawyer, the court, police, and a prosecutor, and it is not closed. When somebody else asks, the court weighs the nature of the case, public safety, and the young person's interest.

keyPhrase.quote: Juvenile records need a real reason.
keyPhrase.gloss: Not open to everybody, not closed to everybody.

scenario.setup: A form at school asking about court history.

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: Can they just look it up?

lines.label: TEACHER
lines.text: Not in Michigan. Not for a juvenile case.

scenario.note: Michigan juvenile records are open only to people the court decides have a real reason.

questions.q: Somebody says they looked up a Michigan kid's juvenile case online. Could they?

options.text: Yes, juvenile cases are public here.
options.explanation: Michigan closed juvenile records in 2021. Before that it was one of the few states where this was possible.

options.text: Only if the kid was charged as an adult.
options.explanation: Being charged as an adult moves a case. It is not what makes an old juvenile record searchable.

options.text: Only after the case is finished.
options.explanation: Finishing a case does not open the file to the public.

questions.hint: This changed recently, and a lot of adults have not caught up.
questions.principle: Michigan used to be one of a handful of states where juvenile court records were public and searchable. A law signed in January 2021 changed that, and since March 2021 only people with a legitimate interest can get at them. Plenty of adults still believe the old rule, which is why somebody may tell you they looked something up and be describing a world that no longer exists.

keyPhrase.quote: Michigan closed juvenile records in 2021.
keyPhrase.gloss: What was true before is not true now.

scenario.setup: A group chat, somebody being confidently wrong.

lines.label: FRIEND
lines.text: You can just search anybody's juvenile case, my cousin did it.

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: Not since 2021 you can't.

scenario.note: Michigan closed juvenile records in 2021. What was true before is not true now.

questions.q: You want a written copy of everything that was said at a hearing. What do you have to do?

options.text: Order a transcript and pay for it.
Ask the clerk for a printout.
options.explanation: A clerk can pull a file. Turning a recording into a written transcript is separate work somebody has to do.

options.text: Ask the court reporter for the file.
options.explanation: The reporter produces a transcript when one is ordered and paid for, rather than handing over a file.
Michigan hearings are not posted online for anybody to replay.

questions.hint: The record exists. Getting a copy is a separate thing.
questions.principle: Everything said gets recorded, and turning that into a written transcript is work somebody has to do and get paid for. In Michigan the rate is set by law: $3.75 per original page since April 2025, with a $50 minimum. A short hearing can therefore cost fifty dollars and a long one considerably more. The record is public. The copy is not free.

keyPhrase.quote: The record is public. The copy costs money.
keyPhrase.gloss: At least fifty dollars in Michigan.

scenario.setup: An argument at home about exactly what a judge said last month.

lines.label: MOM
lines.text: One of us is remembering it wrong.

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: There's a transcript. It costs though.

scenario.note: The record is public. A written copy costs money, at least fifty dollars in Michigan.

questions.q: You are out on bond and you miss a hearing. Who has to be told?

options.text: Nobody. It is between you and the court.
options.explanation: Whoever posted a surety bond has money on the line, so the court has to notify them.
Courts do not contact employers about missed hearings.
Your lawyer finds out, and so does whoever put money up.

questions.hint: Somebody put money up on the promise that you would be there.
questions.principle: In Michigan the court has to notify whoever posted a surety bond within seven days of a failure to appear. That is usually a bondsman, and sometimes it is a family member. Somebody put money on the line for you, and missing a date is the moment they find out. This is the part nobody warns people about.

keyPhrase.quote: Missing a date is not just yours.
keyPhrase.gloss: Whoever posted the bond gets told.

scenario.setup: Your aunt posted bond for a relative and a letter arrives.

lines.label: AUNT
lines.text: Why am I getting this?

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: Because you're the one who put the money up. They have to tell you.

scenario.note: Whoever posted the bond has to be told within seven days of a missed hearing.

questions.q: You get a subpoena in the mail as a witness. What does it require you to do?

options.text: Call and confirm you can make it.
options.explanation: A subpoena is a court order. It is not a scheduling request you can decline.

options.text: Talk to whoever sent it first.
options.explanation: You can talk to whoever sent it, and the order to appear stands either way.

options.text: Nothing, unless you saw something important.
options.explanation: Whether your evidence matters is not yours to decide. Showing up is.

questions.hint: A subpoena is an order, not an invitation.
questions.principle: A subpoena is a court order to appear. Ignoring one can bring a bench warrant or a contempt finding, and a witness can be arrested for not showing. If the date is impossible, that gets sorted with the court or the lawyer who sent it, before the date rather than after.

keyPhrase.quote: A subpoena is an order.
keyPhrase.gloss: Not an invitation, not a request.

scenario.setup: An envelope with a court seal on it. You saw something at a shop.

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: I wasn't even that involved. Do I have to go?

lines.label: MOM
lines.text: It says court on it. You go.

lines.label: YES
lines.text: You turn up and it takes an hour.

lines.label: NO
lines.text: You skip it and the court comes looking.

questions.q: Your lawyer tells you not to bother coming to a scheduling hearing. When does that have to be cleared with the court?

options.text: It does not. Your lawyer can excuse you.
options.explanation: Your lawyer can advise you about it and cannot excuse you from a court's order.
Attendance is set by the court, not by preference.

options.text: Never. Scheduling hearings do not count.
options.explanation: Every hearing on your case counts, including short ones.

questions.hint: A missed hearing is recorded the moment it is missed.
questions.principle: The court sets who has to be there. A lawyer can appear alone for some routine matters and a lawyer's advice about it is worth having, and the court is what decides. Anything worked out afterward is an explanation for something already on the record, which is why it gets sorted before the date rather than after.

keyPhrase.quote: Sort it before, not after.
keyPhrase.gloss: A missed hearing is recorded the moment it is missed.

scenario.setup: A phone call two days before your cousin's hearing.

lines.label: LAWYER
lines.text: It's just scheduling, he doesn't need to come.

lines.label: COUSIN
lines.text: Can you clear that with the court before Thursday?

lines.label: YES
lines.text: It is handled in advance and nothing goes on the record.

lines.label: NO
lines.text: He skips it and it is logged as a failure to appear.

questions.q: You miss your court date. What is the judge likely to issue?

options.text: A new court date in the mail.
options.explanation: Missing a hearing does not get you rescheduled. It usually gets you a warrant.
A fine is not the usual response. An order to arrest you is.
There is no free first miss. The first one can produce a warrant.

questions.hint: The court has one tool for making somebody appear.
questions.principle: Missing a court date usually produces a bench warrant, which is an order for police to arrest you and bring you in. It is called a bench warrant because it comes from the bench rather than from a police investigation. It does not expire on its own and it does not go away because time passed.

keyPhrase.quote: Missing court gets a warrant.
keyPhrase.gloss: Not a reminder, not a new date.

scenario.setup: Your cousin rings at eleven in the morning.

lines.label: COUSIN
lines.text: Court was at nine. I slept through it.

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: Call the lawyer now, not tomorrow.

lines.label: YES
lines.text: Somebody deals with it the same day.

lines.label: NO
lines.text: It sits there for years until it turns up at the worst moment.

questions.q: There is a bench warrant out for you for missing court. When can that turn up?

options.text: Any time an officer runs your name.

options.explanation: A bench warrant sits in a system every officer can search, not in one building.

options.text: Only if you get arrested for something else.
options.explanation: It does not need a new charge to surface. Running your name is enough.
Warrants do not expire on their own. People get picked up on ones years old.

questions.hint: Think about the last time somebody ran a name.
questions.principle: A bench warrant sits in a system every officer can search. A traffic stop, a routine check, an application that runs a background search: any of those can surface it. Warrants do not expire on their own, and people are picked up on ones from years back all the time, usually at the worst possible moment.

keyPhrase.quote: A warrant does not expire.
keyPhrase.gloss: It waits for somebody to run your name.

scenario.setup: Your uncle explaining why he sorted his out straight away.

lines.label: UNCLE
lines.text: It doesn't expire. It just sits there till somebody runs your name.

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: Even years later?

scenario.note: A bench warrant does not expire. It waits for somebody to run your name.

questions.q: In Michigan you are out on bond and you miss a hearing. What can happen besides a warrant?

options.text: Your bond can be taken away.
Nothing else. A warrant is the whole thing.
options.explanation: A warrant is one consequence. The bond money is another.
Missing a hearing does not change what you are charged with.

options.text: Your lawyer gets removed from the case.
options.explanation: Your lawyer stays on the case. The money is what is at risk.

questions.hint: Somebody's money is riding on you being there.
questions.principle: A Michigan court can revoke release and declare the bond money forfeited when somebody fails to appear. That money is gone, and it is often a family member's. Only a judge can sign that order, not a magistrate. If the person turns up within a set window there is a process for arguing it back, which is one reason dealing with a missed date fast matters.

keyPhrase.quote: Missing a hearing can cost the bond money.
keyPhrase.gloss: Usually somebody else's money.

scenario.setup: A friend's older brother missed a court date last year.

lines.label: FRIEND
lines.text: They took the bond money back. My mum had put it up.

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: That's why they wanted him there.

scenario.note: Missing a hearing can cost the bond money, and it is often somebody else's.
